cards.front: Properties an ID scheme might need
cards.back: Unique, no coordination per ID, roughly time-sorted, compact (64 bits) and unguessable. They pull against each other, so decide which you actually need first.

cards.front: Why can't IDs be both time-sorted and unguessable?
cards.back: If IDs grow with time, an attacker can narrow down the next one. For public links, keep a sortable internal ID and hand out a separate random token.
Flickr's tiny MySQL database whose only job is a counter. Two of them, one handing out odd numbers and one even, remove the single point of failure, but each ID still costs a network hop.
Each app server leases a block of IDs, say 1,000, from a coordinator and hands them out from memory. A crashed server just leaves a gap, which is fine because IDs must be unique, not gap-free.
UUIDv4 is 122 random bits and is not time-ordered. UUIDv7 starts with a 48-bit millisecond timestamp, so it sorts by time and inserts land at the right edge of a B-tree, but it leaks creation time.
A 64-bit integer: 41 bits of milliseconds since a custom epoch, 10 bits of machine ID and 12 bits of sequence. That gives about 70 years, 1,024 generators and 4,096 IDs per millisecond each.

cards.front: Why send 64-bit IDs to browsers as strings?
cards.back: They exceed JavaScript's largest safe integer (2^53 − 1), so parsing them as numbers rounds the last digits. That is why Twitter's API returned both id and id_str.

cards.front: Are Snowflake IDs strictly ordered across machines?
cards.back: No. Clocks on different machines differ by a few milliseconds, so IDs are only roughly time-ordered (k-sorted) across machines and strictly ordered within one generator.

cards.front: What should a Snowflake generator do if the clock goes backwards?
cards.back: Remember the last millisecond used. If the clock reads earlier, wait if the gap is a few milliseconds, or refuse to issue IDs and alert if it is large.

cards.front: Why do sortable IDs help B-tree storage?
cards.back: Ordered inserts go to the right-hand edge, so pages split less, stay fuller and only the edge needs to stay in memory. Random keys split pages in the middle and need the whole index cached.

cards.front: The catch with increasing IDs on range-sharded stores
cards.back: On Bigtable, HBase, Spanner or CockroachDB, ever-increasing keys all go to the last range, which becomes a write hot spot. Hash the key, add a shard prefix or use a random ID there.

Two generators with the same machine ID, from a config typo or a cloned VM. Assign machine IDs from something that enforces uniqueness, like an etcd lease or a StatefulSet ordinal, and keep the primary key constraint.

quiz.q: How many IDs can a single standard Snowflake generator make per millisecond?
quiz.why: The 12-bit sequence allows 2^12 = 4,096 IDs per millisecond.

quiz.q: Why pick a recent custom epoch for a 41-bit millisecond timestamp instead of 1970?
choices: Counting from 1970 would already have used about 56 of the 69.7 years
Unix time is not available in milliseconds
It lets more machines share the ID space
quiz.why: 41 bits of milliseconds last 69.7 years from whatever epoch you choose.

quiz.q: A server leasing blocks of 1,000 IDs writes 5,000 rows a second. How often does it call the coordinator?
quiz.why: 5,000 IDs a second divided by 1,000 IDs a block is five leases a second.

quiz.q: Which ID type causes inserts to land all over a B-tree index?
quiz.why: UUIDv4 is completely random, while the others grow with time.

quiz.q: Two writes happen on different servers a millisecond apart. Can you trust their Snowflake IDs to say which came first?
choices: No, clock differences make cross-machine order only rough
Yes, IDs are strictly ordered everywhere
Yes, if both servers use NTP
Only if the machine IDs are adjacent
quiz.why: Snowflake IDs are k-sorted across machines; use a version number or single sequencer for ordering.

quiz.q: Why should a business never promise gap-free IDs from a distributed scheme?
choices: Rollbacks, crashes and abandoned blocks all leave holes
quiz.why: If consecutive numbers are truly needed, make them a separate, slow, serialised counter.

quiz.q: Sequential order IDs leak what to competitors?
choices: How many orders you take per day
quiz.why: Place two orders a day apart and subtract the IDs.
